Car Culture

Everything Is Two Cars

America invented the pickup, walled it off in 1964, and has been coasting ever since

The Volkswagen is a Ford. The Mazda is an Isuzu. The Nissan is a Mitsubishi. Outside North America, almost every pickup is two or three vehicles wearing different faces — and that is not a sign of laziness. It is what a market looks like when it is too competitive for anyone to survive alone.

By Margot Devries  ·  Car Culture  ·  38 min read

Park a Volkswagen Amarok beside a Ford Ranger and look at the door handles. Then the mirrors, the glasshouse, the way the bed sides meet the cab. By the time you reach the dashboard you will have stopped pretending. They are the same truck, built on the same line, differing chiefly in the sheet metal ahead of the windshield and the badge on the tailgate.

Americans tend to read that as cynicism. It is the opposite. Volkswagen does not build its own pickup because in the market where pickups are genuinely fought over, Volkswagen cannot afford to. Neither can Nissan. Mazda gave up years ago. Twenty-odd trucks are grinding each other's margins down to nothing, and only the volume leaders can still fund a platform of their own.

Now look at the United States. Five mid-size trucks. No diesel. No plug-in hybrid. No price pressure from underneath. Margins fat enough that nobody has to try very hard, and a national conviction that we are the truck capital of the world.

We are not. We are the truck capital of nowhere but here, and we have been since a Tuesday in December 1963.

01The Chicken War, and what it bought

In 1962 the European Economic Community's Common Agricultural Policy tripled West German tariffs on poultry, from 4.5 cents a pound to 13.5. The target was American chicken, which industrial farming had made so cheap that European producers were being wiped out. It worked. By mid-1963 US chicken exports to Europe had fallen sixty-seven percent.

The press called it the Chicken War, which remains one of the great acts of false advertising in the history of journalism.

Because say it out loud and tell me you do not want ringside seats. East meets West. General Tso versus Colonel Sanders. Twelve herbs and spices against sweet, savory, tangy and that slow chili burn arriving three seconds after you have already committed. Two corner men, two philosophies, one pressure fryer. The purse goes to the promoter, the belt goes to whoever is still standing, and the winner — the actual, undisputed winner — is your mouth.

It gets better, because neither man was ever entitled to the rank. Colonel Sanders was a Kentucky Colonel, an honorary title handed out by the governor to people the state likes, which confers the authority to be called Colonel and absolutely nothing else. General Tso was a real Qing dynasty commander who put down a rebellion, ran a province, and went to his grave in 1885 having never eaten, seen, heard of, or been in the same century as the dish. Two fake officers, no chain of command between them, fronting a war fought entirely by trade ministers with clipboards.

The reality, inevitably, was tariff schedules. It ran hot enough that a senator from Arkansas interrupted a NATO nuclear weapons debate in Geneva to complain about it, which is the single most American sentence in this article — a man rising in the middle of a conversation about the survival of Western Europe to raise the matter of poultry. Kennedy was working the diplomatic angle when he was assassinated in November 1963.

Less than two weeks after being sworn in, on December 4, 1963, Lyndon Johnson signed Proclamation 3564, effective the following January. It imposed a 25 percent duty — roughly ten times the average American tariff of the day — on four categories of goods.

Potato starch. Dextrin. Brandy. And light trucks.

Read that list again. Three of them are ingredients. One of them is a Ford F-250. Nobody in 1963 thought that was a coincidence, and nobody has since.

What the fourth item was actually for Historians broadly agree the truck clause was a concession to Walter Reuther, president of the United Auto Workers. The UAW had assembled a $59 million strike fund — more than $600 million in today's money — pointed at 1964, an election year. Johnson needed the union's backing for the Civil Rights Act and could not afford a strike. Reuther wanted Volkswagen stopped.

The specific irritant was the VW Type 2, the Transporter, which in pickup and van form had reached just under 37,000 US registrations in 1963 and revealed a market Detroit had either not noticed or not bothered with. Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act six months later.

The brandy tariff went away. So did dextrin and potato starch, negotiated off in the Kennedy and Tokyo rounds. The truck tariff never did. Sixty-two years on, a 25 percent duty imposed over frozen chicken and a labor negotiation is still the single most important fact about the American pickup market — and the reason a passenger car enters the country at 2.5 percent while a pickup pays eleven times that.

Keep one detail in your pocket for later. The tariff was written to stop a Volkswagen.

02Why a ute is not a pickup

Around 1932, in Gippsland, Victoria, a farmer's wife wrote a letter to Hubert French, the managing director of Ford Australia.

Her problem was Depression arithmetic. Banks would finance one vehicle, not two, so the family car was an open-sided farm truck, and every Sunday she arrived at church wet. Her request, as the designer who answered it recalled decades later, was for a vehicle to go to church in on a Sunday and which can carry our pigs to market on Mondays.

The letter went from French to his sales manager, to the plant superintendent, and finally to a 22-year-old designer at the Geelong plant named Lew Bandt. Bandt took a Ford coupe, shortened the cabin, strengthened the chassis and molded a steel tray onto the back with a hinged tailgate. The coupe utility went into production in 1934. When Henry Ford saw one, he called it a Kangaroo Chaser. Bandt died in 1987, driving a replica of his own creation.

"Coupe utility" was far too many syllables for Australians, who abbreviate everything and staple an -o or an -ie to the end of it. The service station is a servo. The afternoon is the arvo. The liquor store is a bottle-o, the sunglasses are sunnies, the barbecue is a barbie, the mosquitoes are mozzies and McDonald's is, universally, Maccas. Utility became ute, and never went back. Australians would abbreviate their own names if they could, and to be fair, they largely have.

A pickup is named for a job. A ute is named for a compromise — and the compromise turned out to be the harder engineering problem.

That is not wordplay. It is the whole difference between the two markets, sitting in the two words.

Pickup describes an action: a truck you pick loads up with. It is a tool, and America has always treated it as one — a second vehicle, bought alongside the family car, judged on how much it can haul.

Ute describes a purpose: utility, singular, one vehicle doing every job there is. It was born from a woman who could only afford one vehicle and needed it to be two, and ninety years later that is still precisely the brief. The modern global ute is a dual cab with five seats and coil springs, expected to carry a crew and a load Monday through Friday, tow three and a half tons on Saturday, and take the family to dinner on Sunday without anyone complaining about the ride.

Ask a vehicle to be a truck and it will be a good truck. Ask it to be everything, in a market where twenty rivals are being asked the same thing, and you get something considerably more sophisticated.

03What a ute has to be

The rules of this market are mostly unwritten and completely non-negotiable. Miss one and you are not a serious entrant, regardless of how good the truck is.

7,716 pounds braked

Three and a half metric tons. It is the maximum a standard Australian driver's license permits behind a vehicle, which means it is the number the entire industry engineers toward. There is no credit for 3,200 and no glory in 3,700. You hit the number or you are explaining yourself. This is why the BYD Shark 6 arriving at 5,500 pounds was treated as a scandal rather than a footnote, and why BYD spent two model years fixing it.

A one-ton payload, nominally

The class is still called the one-ton segment, most dual-cabs no longer manage a ton, and everyone keeps using the name anyway. What matters more is the arithmetic that follows: subtract the towball download of a 7,716-pound trailer — typically 770 pounds — and whatever is left is what you may legally put in the vehicle. Buyers in this market do that sum in the showroom. American buyers almost never do.

Dual cab, four doors, five seats

Single-cab work trucks still exist and still sell to fleets, but the segment is overwhelmingly the family-and-trade compromise. That is also why the wagon spin-offs exist — the seven-seat 4x4s we covered separately are simply the next step for a family that outgrew the tray.

The tray is a platform, not a bed

This one has no American equivalent. Most of these trucks are sold in cab-chassis form — no bed at all — and an entire industry exists to bolt on what you actually need: an aluminum tray, a service body, a canopy, a slide-out drawer system, a dual battery setup, a water tank. Buy a bare cab-chassis, choose your tray, and the vehicle becomes whatever the job is. American trucks come with the bed welded to the decision.

Five ANCAP stars

Fleet tenders and mining contracts now routinely require a five-star safety rating, which makes it a commercial requirement rather than a marketing bullet. A ute that cannot get five stars cannot be sold to the customers who buy in fifties.

The warranty war

Five years became standard, then seven. GWM offers seven with unlimited kilometers. That is not generosity — it is a Chinese entrant buying credibility it has not yet earned, and it has dragged the whole segment along with it.

Diesel, until about eighteen months ago

Torque under load, range between fuel stops, and availability in places where the pump is a drum on a farm. This was the one unshakeable assumption in the segment, and the last two years have blown a hole straight through it.

04Everything is two cars

Here is the map. Learn it once and the entire market becomes legible.

Who is actually who
The donorThe twinNotes
Ford Ranger (T6.2)Volkswagen AmarokAlso underpins the Ford Everest
Isuzu D-MaxMazda BT-50The BT-50 used to be a Ranger. It changed families in 2020
Mitsubishi TritonNissan Navara (D27)New for 2026. Also underpins the Pajero Sport
LDV Terron 9MG U9The Chinese entrants do it too

The logic is sound and slightly brutal. A ladder-frame truck is enormously expensive to engineer, crash-test and homologate, and its buyers are conservative enough that novelty is a liability. Amortize that across two brands and two dealer networks and the risk halves. Volkswagen gets a competitive ute without funding one. Ford gets volume. Everyone eats.

Except it does not work equally well for everybody, and the punishment is savage. 4X4 Australia, reviewing the new Navara, laid it out: since the Amarok stopped being a Volkswagen design and became a rebadged Ranger, VW has been selling roughly one Amarok for every ten Rangers. The badge that was meant to be the sophisticated alternative became the version nobody buys.

The BT-50 tells the same story from the other direction. It used to be a Ranger and sold strongly; it became a D-Max and a chunk of its following never forgave it. And the cautionary tale everyone in the industry cites is the Mercedes-Benz X-Class — a Nissan Navara in a three-pointed star, priced like a Mercedes, dead in barely three years.

Which makes the 2026 Navara a genuinely interesting bet. Nissan is not the donor this time; it is the passenger, riding on Mitsubishi's Triton. Its answer to the badge problem is engineering: locally retuned suspension developed with the Australian firm Premcar, and a Warrior version with 32.2-inch all-terrains, a wider track, a lift and a multi-stage bash plate system. Volkswagen is playing the identical card with a Walkinshaw-tuned Amarok. Both companies have concluded that if you cannot own the platform, you had better own the tune.

Now notice what none of this has in common with the United States. Nobody in America shares a truck platform across brands, because nobody has to. There is no margin pressure severe enough to force it.

05Why Thailand builds the world's trucks

Nearly every vehicle in this article is built in Thailand, and most of the rest in South Africa.

Thailand's nickname in the trade is the Detroit of Asia and it was earned deliberately — decades of industrial policy built a supplier base, a skilled workforce and export infrastructure specifically around one-ton pickups. Toyota builds the HiLux at Samrong. Isuzu builds the D-Max at Samut Prakan. Ford builds the Ranger and Everest at Rayong. Mitsubishi builds the Triton at Laem Chabang. From there they go to Australia, New Zealand, Southeast Asia, the Middle East, Africa, Latin America and Europe.

Which is exactly why none of it reaches America. Twenty-five percent, at the dock, on everything.

06The establishment

Ford Ranger — the one that changed the rules

Donor platform · Rayong, Thailand and Silverton, South Africa · from about A$40,000

The Ranger leads the segment because it stopped behaving like a work truck. The T6.2 generation was developed in Australia, spans bare XL cab-chassis to Wildtrak X, Platinum and Raptor, and offers a 3.0-liter turbodiesel V6 that nothing else in the mainstream class can answer. It took 17,257 deliveries in the first half of 2026.

What it is like: the most car-like of the mainstream diesels, quiet at a highway cruise, with the V6 making towing genuinely relaxed rather than merely possible. The trade is price and a slightly synthetic feel to the steering. Who buys it: everyone, which is the point — tradies at the bottom, families in the middle, and people who want a Raptor at the top. Off road: excellent in Wildtrak and better in Raptor, though a Raptor's soft long-travel setup is a desert weapon rather than a rock crawler.

Toyota HiLux — the one that will not die

IMV platform · Samrong, Thailand · from A$45,990

Toyota sold 51,297 internal-combustion HiLuxes in Australia in a single year. The 2.8-liter 1GD-FTV diesel is documented running past 310,000 miles and shares parts with the Fortuner, which means a mechanic anywhere from Broome to Botswana can keep one alive with what is already on the shelf.

What it is like: noisier, firmer and less sophisticated than a Ranger, and its owners regard that as evidence of seriousness. Who buys it: fleets, miners, farmers, and anyone whose calculation is about the fifteenth year rather than the first. The electrification tell: Toyota launched a battery-electric HiLux aimed at government and mining fleets at roughly A$17,000 above the diesel, and expects to sell about 500 of them in 2026. Against 51,297 diesels. That is not a transition; that is a toe in the water with the other foot nailed to the dock.

Isuzu D-Max — the tradesman's truck

Donor platform · Samut Prakan, Thailand · from A$46,200

Isuzu builds trucks — actual trucks, the kind with air brakes — and the D-Max is what that heritage produces when scaled down. The 3.0-liter four makes 188 hp and 332 lb-ft, which is unremarkable, attached to a reputation for indifference to abuse, which is not.

What it is like: agricultural in the good sense. The engine is loud and unbothered, the six-speed is slow-witted, and nothing about it feels fragile. Off road: a simple part-time system with no center differential — engage on dirt, disengage before pavement or you will wind up the driveline. Some buyers call that a flaw; others call it one less thing to break at two hundred and fifty miles from a phone. Who buys it: people for whom the truck is a tool and downtime is the only metric that matters.

Mazda BT-50 — the D-Max in a better suit

D-Max twin · from about A$47,000

The BT-50's whole story is that it used to be a Ranger. Two generations of buyers learned to love a Mazda that drove like a Ford, and in 2020 Mazda switched partners to Isuzu. What you get now is D-Max mechanicals under sheet metal and an interior that are noticeably more considered — softer materials, better design language, a nicer place to sit.

Who buys it: someone who wants D-Max durability without D-Max austerity, and does not mind that the enthusiast forums still grumble. It is the most improved-feeling truck in the class relative to its donor, and it is also the clearest evidence that badge engineering only works when the twin brings something the donor lacks.

Mitsubishi Triton — the clever one

Donor platform · Laem Chabang, Thailand · from about A$45,000

The Triton undercuts nearly everything and carries the segment's smartest transfer case. Super Select 4WD-II gives four positions: 2H, 4H with an open center differential, 4HLc locked, and 4LLc low range. That 4H is the trick — genuine four-wheel drive you can leave engaged on dry pavement indefinitely, for wet roads, gravel and towing, which almost nothing else in this class can do. It is the same lineage we have written about at length, and it now underpins both the Pajero Sport and the Navara.

What it is like: narrower than the Ranger, which makes it easier in a city and on a tight trail, at some cost in cabin width. The 2.4-liter bi-turbo is the weak link — adequate rather than muscular. Who buys it: the value shopper who has actually read the spec sheet.

Nissan Navara — the passenger

Triton twin · from about A$50,000

The D27 Navara is a Triton with Nissan's face, launched into Australia in early 2026 after the previous car's sales had slowed to nothing. Nissan's defense is Premcar's local suspension tuning and a forthcoming Warrior with real off-road hardware. Whether that is enough is the open question of the segment — the Amarok's ten-to-one deficit suggests buyers can smell a rebadge from some distance.

Volkswagen Amarok — the cautionary tale

Ranger twin · Silverton, South Africa · from about A$55,000

The first Amarok was a genuine Volkswagen, a properly engineered ute with a V6 that people loved. The second is a Ranger. It is a good truck — 2.0 bi-turbo at 201 horsepower and 369 lb-ft on a ten-speed, or the same 3.0 V6 diesel — and Volkswagen sells one for every ten Rangers built beside it. A Walkinshaw-tuned version is coming to give it an identity of its own. It needs one.

07The invasion

In 2025 a battery company that had never built a pickup launched one, and the segment has not settled since.

The BYD Shark 6 is a plug-in hybrid dual-cab: a 29.6 kWh battery, about 60 miles of electric-only range on the generous NEDC cycle, and a combined 430 horsepower and 479 lb-ft — more than a Ranger Raptor. From A$57,900.

It sold more than 15,000 units in Australia in its first year and reached third best-selling ute in the country by mid-2026, ahead of the D-Max and the Triton, taking 3,398 sales in June alone and finishing sixth outright among all vehicles that month.

It also arrived violating the segment's one absolute rule, towing only 5,500 pounds, and BYD has spent two model years fixing it. The 2026 range now runs from a A$55,900 Dynamic cab-chassis through the A$57,900 Premium to a A$62,900 Performance grade that finally delivers the full 7,716 pounds and a turbocharged 2.0-liter Super Hybrid drivetrain.

What that did to everyone else GWM's Cannon Alpha PHEV landed at about A$59,990 with the full 7,716-pound rating. Ford answered with a Ranger PHEV from A$71,990 to A$86,990. GWM's conventional Cannon undercuts the establishment at roughly A$39,490 for a loaded diesel dual-cab with leather, a 360-degree camera and a seven-year warranty. Kia arrived with the Tasman, MG and LDV with the U9 and Terron 9, and Chery has a diesel-electric ute coming claiming 469 horsepower and 590 lb-ft.

Read the pricing twice and the problem is unmissable: Ford's cheapest plug-in ute costs more than BYD's most expensive one.

The counter-argument deserves its say, because Australian buyers are making it loudly and it is not stupid. The Shark 6 cooled through 2026 after its breakout year. Nobody knows what a Chinese plug-in ute is worth at eight years old, or what a 29.6 kWh battery looks like after a decade of 45-degree summers and corrugated dirt. In a segment where people keep vehicles fifteen years and drive them a thousand kilometers from the nearest dealer, an unproven drivetrain is a genuine risk. That is precisely the bet Toyota is making by selling 500 electric HiLuxes to fleets and 51,000 diesels to everyone else.

But notice what is happening regardless. The establishment is being forced to respond — on price, on warranty, on powertrain, within eighteen months. That is what a competitive market does to incumbents.

Read down the torque column. Every global diesel matches or beats the American gasoline engines on the number that actually matters when a trailer is attached, while using roughly a third less fuel to do it. Read down the towing column and America is competitive. Read the economy column and it is not close.

And then read the last two rows of the global half. A plug-in hybrid making 430 horsepower with a hundred kilometers of electric range, and a diesel four-cylinder returning something near 30 mpg, both for less than a Tacoma.

09The Ranger test

If you want the argument compressed into a single vehicle, Ford has helpfully provided one.

Ford builds the Ranger on the T6.2 platform for the entire world. In Australia, Thailand, South Africa and across Europe, the good one has a 3.0-liter turbodiesel V6 making 247 horsepower and 443 lb-ft, tows 7,716 pounds, and returns something in the region of 26 miles per gallon. In the United States, the same truck from the same company offers a 2.3-liter gasoline four or a 2.7-liter gasoline V6, tows 7,500 pounds, and manages 23 mpg on a friendlier test cycle.

More torque, more towing, better economy, longer proven service life — and Americans cannot buy it.

Not because Ford lacks the engineering. Not because the diesel could not be federalized; Ford has certified diesels here before and builds the American Ranger in Wayne, Michigan on the same architecture. It is not offered because nothing is forcing Ford to offer it. There is no rival in the American mid-size class fielding a diesel V6, because the rivals who build one cannot get it through the door at 25 percent, so the competitive pressure that would make Ford bother simply does not exist.

The same company builds a better Ranger for the rest of the world. It declines to sell it to the market that supposedly loves trucks most, because nobody here is making it.

That is what protection actually purchased. Not American jobs in any straightforward sense — the Tacoma is built in Mexico, the Ranger in Michigan, the Frontier in Tennessee, and the tariff has done nothing to settle where anyone builds anything. What it bought was the absence of pressure: a market where five trucks compete gently, prices climb annually, engines stay gasoline, and no Chinese entrant can arrive with a seven-year warranty and force everyone else to match it.

10The reckoning

Americans buy more pickups than anybody. Roughly one in five new vehicles sold here is a truck, the F-Series has led the market for four decades, and the cultural position of the pickup is unmatched anywhere on earth.

All of that is true, and none of it is the same thing as having the best trucks.

The rest of the world argues about twenty of them, across four drivetrains, from thirty-four thousand dollars to a hundred and seventy-three, with diesel V6s and plug-in hybrids and seven-year warranties, in a fight so tight that Volkswagen and Nissan have both concluded they cannot afford to build their own. America has five, all gasoline, all made in North America, at prices that only go up.

The most competitive vehicle segment on the planet is one Americans are legally walled off from — by a proclamation signed to settle a dispute about poultry, as a favor to a union that no longer exists in the form that asked for it, against a company whose modern pickup still cannot be sold here.

Volkswagen builds the Amarok. It is a very good truck. Sixty-two years after Lyndon Johnson signed a piece of paper specifically to keep Volkswagen trucks out of America, it has never been offered for sale in the United States, in either of its two generations.

The tariff worked. That is the problem.

The verdict

Badge engineering is not a symptom of laziness. It is a symptom of competition so severe that only the volume leaders can still fund a platform, and it has produced a generation of trucks better than anything sold in the country that invented the pickup. The Ranger is the finest of them and the HiLux will outlive them all. The Shark 6 is the most disruptive vehicle to arrive in the class in a decade and nobody yet knows what it is worth used. Meanwhile America, holding the world's largest truck market and its smallest set of choices, has spent sixty-two years congratulating itself on a tariff that stopped a Volkswagen and accidentally stopped everything else too.
